title: The Gita begins in grief
hookLine: the Gita opens with a general's briefing and a wall of conches, and its first chapter ends with Arjuna sitting down in grief.
carry: the gita's first yoga is honest grief
tomorrow: The self that is never killed

cards: Ask someone how the Bhagavad Gita begins, and they may tell you about Krishna's teaching. But after the old king's question, the first real speech belongs to Duryodhana, briefing his old teacher Drona.
It sounds like a general's report. Today: the noise before the silence.

teach.b: Duryodhana stands before Drona and points across the field. Look at the Pandava army, he says, arrayed by your own student. Then he tells everyone to guard Bhishma.
Bhishma doesn't answer in words. To cheer him, the old grandsire roars like a lion and blows his conch, and the field erupts. Krishna blows his conch, Panchajanya.
Arjuna blows his, Devadatta. The Gita says the sound made earth and sky resound. Then Arjuna asks Krishna to drive the chariot out between the armies, so he can see who he's about to fight.
Krishna sets it down in front of Bhishma and Drona.
Friends. His limbs give way. His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and he sits down in the chariot, overwhelmed with grief.
Here's the surprising part. In the Gita as it's traditionally recited, every chapter closes with a title, and every title calls that chapter a yoga, a path to God.
This one is called Arjuna Vishada Yoga: the yoga of Arjuna's despair. The hero is in tears, and the tradition still counts it as a path.
Many teachers read it this way: honest grief is the doorway, because a man who thinks he has every answer never asks for a teacher. Krishna doesn't start teaching here.
He waits, and in the next chapter, when Arjuna admits he is lost and asks to be taught, the Gita's great teaching begins.
That's one reason so many Hindus turn to the Gita in their hardest weeks: a loss, a family fight, a week that crushes you. It doesn't begin with a hero who has it together.
It begins with someone who can't go on, and calls that the first step.

how: In the traditionally recited Gita, each chapter closes with a title naming it a yoga; the first is Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair, and the conches it names, like Krishna's Panchajanya, are familiar from pictures of Krishna and Arjuna in the chariot.

games.q: you're Arjuna. the conches have sounded. you ask Krishna to drive you between the armies, and you see your grandfather and teachers. what do you do?
o: drop your bow and sit down in the chariot.
turn the chariot and leave the field.
games.why: his bow slips from his hand, and he sits down in grief. the tradition calls this chapter a yoga: honest despair is where the teaching begins.

practice: Sit the way Arjuna sat, set down in the chariot. Breathing in, name honestly one thing that feels too heavy right now; you don't have to fix it. Breathing out, set it down beside you, the way he set down his bow.
Many Hindus bring a heavy heart to Krishna just like this, before asking for anything. If you pray, tell God plainly what's heavy. If you don't, simply let it be named.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma Parva. The book named for the grandsire, whose conch started the noise that ends in Arjuna's grief, and the Gita's first yoga.
